analysis.one_liner: Eases OSHA workplace-safety inspections, penalties, and employer liability while extending coverage to federal workers.
analysis.headline: Introduced by Sen. Kassebaum with Sen. Hatch on March 17, 1994, referred to the Senate Labor Committee, which held one hearing on March 22 and never voted; the bill died when the 103rd Congress ended in January 1995.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite the Occupational Safety and Health Act. It would exempt many small employers, farms, and low-injury industries from routine safety inspections, let employers earn blanket exemption from OSHA inspections through private consultation programs or good safety records, cap most civil penalties at $7,000, and give employers new defenses against citations, including an 'employee misconduct' defense. It would also require states to make their hazard-labeling rules identical to federal standards and loosen restrictions on employer-run safety committees. Alongside those employer gains, it would extend OSHA protection to federal employees for the first time, mandate investigations of all workplace deaths, extend the deadline for workers to file retaliation complaints, and add small-business training and assistance programs.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers subject to OSHA, especially small businesses, farms without labor camps, and industries with below-average injury rates, would gain exemption from routine inspections, a hard $7,000 penalty cap with reductions of 25-50% for having safety programs, new legal defenses, and freedom from citations while variance requests are pending. Insurance carriers and private safety consultants would gain a new role: their certification programs would qualify employers for the blanket inspection exemption. Employers would also gain authority to run workplace alcohol and drug testing programs.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Employers, especially small firms and farms

how_it_helps.text: Exempts employers with 10 or fewer employees in low-injury industries, and farms without temporary labor camps, from routine OSHA inspections, though inspections still occur after complaints, fatalities, or hospitalizing incidents.

Creates a voluntary program granting employers exemption from all routine inspections if they use approved consultation or certification programs, including programs run by insurance carriers, or maintain an exemplary safety record with employee participation.

Caps most civil penalties at $7,000, strikes the higher penalties for willful and repeat violations, and cuts penalties 25-50% for employers with safety programs or exemplary records, while allowing multipliers up to 10x for fatalities and patterns of violations.

Gives employers new defenses: no citation without employer knowledge of the hazard, an 'employee misconduct' defense where workers were trained and rules enforced, and vacating citations where alternative methods were equally protective.
Makes the National Labor Relations Act's ban on employer-dominated organizations inapplicable to employer health and safety committees.
Authorizes employer alcohol and drug testing programs and pre-employment testing under Labor Department standards.
Extends OSHA coverage to executive, judicial, and legislative branch employees, including congressional workers, who were previously covered by a separate, weaker regime.

Mandates investigation of every work-related death and serious incident, extends whistleblower complaint deadlines to 60 days with mediation options, and gives injured workers and families access to case information.

analysis.who_pays: Workers would bear the cost in the form of less government oversight: the employers most likely to be exempted are precisely those whose own reporting shows few injuries, and self-inspection replaces unannounced federal checks. Families of workers killed or hurt in exempted workplaces would lose the independent investigation that current routine inspections provide. Workers could also face employer testing programs and employer-run safety committees without union protections. States would lose the ability to require hazard labeling and information rules stricter than federal standards.

drawbacks.text: The exemption from routine inspections depends on employer injury and lost-workday data, which reflect what employers report; workplaces with unreported hazards could qualify for exemption precisely because their hazards are not being counted.

Capping penalties at $7,000 and striking the willful and repeat violation provisions removes the strongest financial deterrent for employers who knowingly gamble on worker safety, though the bill allows up to 10x multipliers for fatalities and patterns.
The employee-misconduct defense could let employers avoid citations by blaming workers, even where the underlying hazard or inadequate staffing contributed to the violation.

Requiring state hazard-labeling and information requirements to be identical to federal OSHA standards would preempt stricter state right-to-know laws that currently give workers more information about chemical hazards.

Exempting employer-run health and safety committees from National Labor Relations Act restrictions raises the concern that such committees can function as management-controlled substitutes for independent unions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill mixes real improvements for workers—federal employee coverage, mandatory death investigations, longer retaliation-complaint windows, victim information rights, and targeted small-business help—into a bill whose central architecture is a broad rollback of inspections, penalties, and employer liability. The exemption pathways, penalty cap, and new defenses would have materially weakened independent oversight of workplace safety, and the state preemption provision would have rolled back stronger state rules. On balance, the rollback provisions were the core of the bill and outweighed the worker-side benefits.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate referred it to the Labor and Human Resources Committee, which held a single hearing in March 1994, and the bill never reached a markup or a floor vote before the 103rd Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Nancy Kassebaum, joined by Sen. Orrin Hatch, introduced the Occupational Safety and Health Reform Act on March 17, 1994.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources.
The committee held hearings on March 22, 1994, but took no further action on the bill.
No version of the bill was ever reported out of committee or voted on by either chamber, and it expired when the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Workers kept the existing OSHA enforcement structure: routine inspections, the willful-violation penalty framework, and independent federal oversight of workplace hazards all remained in place because the bill never advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Workers, who kept existing safety protections

for.name: Sen. Nancy Kassebaum
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on March 17, 1994.

for.name: Sen. Orrin Hatch
for.what_they_did: Joined Kassebaum in introducing the bill.

for.name: Employer trade groups
for.role: Business associations supporting OSHA regulatory relief
for.what_they_did: Backed OSHA reform legislation in the mid-1990s that would ease inspection and penalty requirements for employers.

against.name: Sen. Edward Kennedy
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee of referral, allowed only a hearing on March 22, 1994; the committee never marked up or reported the bill.

against.name: Organized labor
against.what_they_did: Opposed legislation of this period that would roll back OSHA inspections, penalties, and employer liability.

sides.party_line_note: Both sponsors were Republicans in a Democratic-led Senate; the bill received no roll-call votes, so the partisan split never had a chance to show itself on the record.

industries.industry: Employers subject to OSHA (especially small firms, farms, and low-injury industries)
industries.note: The bill exempts them from routine inspections, caps penalties, and adds defenses to citations, shifting safety oversight from government inspectors to employers' own programs and self-reported records.

industries.industry: Insurance carriers and private safety-consultation firms
industries.note: Their certification and consultation programs would qualify employers for blanket exemption from OSHA inspections, making paid private review the gatekeeper in place of unannounced federal inspections.
The bill authorizes employer testing programs, including random and pre-employment testing, creating a larger market for testing services at workers' expense of privacy.
The bill exempts employer health and safety committees from NLRA restrictions on employer-dominated organizations, a structure unions view as displacing independent worker representation.
